# Fixed Timestep Simulation

Advance the simulation in constant-size steps regardless of how long a frame took. The alternative —
stepping by the real elapsed delta — makes physics a function of hardware: the same jump reaches a
different height on a faster machine, and the same movement code on client and server produces
different answers.

For a networked game this is not a polish issue but a correctness precondition. Prediction under
[[client-side-prediction-and-reconciliation]] only converges if both copies of the movement code step
at the same rate; if the rates differ, prediction error accumulates with no bound. In [[stickfps]] it
is a named hard constraint (C3), 60 Hz on **both** sides.

## Two implementations, because the hosts differ

**Server — drift-corrected recursive `setTimeout`, explicitly not `setInterval`.** `setInterval`
schedules against its own start time and silently coalesces or drops ticks when the event loop is
busy, so the loop slowly slides against wall time and there is no signal that it has. The recursive
form measures how late the current tick actually was and subtracts that from the next delay, so drift
is corrected every tick rather than compounding.

**Client — an accumulator over the render loop.** Each frame adds its delta to an accumulator and
drains it in whole steps; the leftover carries to the next frame. The step count per frame is
**capped at 5**, which is the standard defence against the spiral of death: without a cap, a frame
that took 2 s queues 120 steps, which takes longer than a frame, which queues more steps.

## The cap has a visible consequence

Capping means that when the renderer falls far enough behind, **simulated time runs slower than wall
time** — steps are discarded, not deferred. In [[stickfps]] this showed up concretely: under headless
software GL the simulation advanced at roughly 40% of wall time, so [[playwright]] runs measuring
round timers or reload durations against real seconds were wrong for a reason that had nothing to do
with the product.

That is the trade-off in one sentence: **a fixed timestep guarantees determinism per step, not that
the simulation keeps up with the clock.** Anything that must track wall time — round timers, fuses,
cooldowns — has to be reasoned about separately, or authored server-side where the loop is drift
corrected. [[stickfps]] does the latter; all timing that scores anything lives under
[[server-authoritative-netcode]].

## What it buys elsewhere

Deterministic steps make the simulation unit-testable without a renderer: the movement controller,
the weapon state machine and the spring integrator in [[stickfps]] are all tested as pure functions
stepped N times, which is why the client test suite can cover them at all under [[vite]]'s vitest.
